findings.source_passage: The traveller in the south must often have remarked that peculiar air of refinement, that softness of voice and manner, which seems in many cases to be a particular gift to the quadroon and mulatto women.
findings.source_locator: Paragraph 2, opening of the ethnographic digression
findings.why_it_matters: The narratorial address to 'the traveller in the south' is a distinctive voice-establishing move — it positions the narrator as eye-witness sociologist and implicates the reader's assumed experience. The draft collapses this into a bare descriptor, erasing the rhetorical frame.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full sentence opening 'The traveller in the south must often have remarked…' to preserve the narrator's sociological voice and the reader-implicating address.

findings.source_passage: These natural graces in the quadroon are often united with beauty of the most dazzling kind, and in almost every case with a personal appearance prepossessing and agreeable.
findings.source_locator: Paragraph 2, second sentence of the ethnographic digression
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence extends the narrator's deliberate socio-ethnographic register, a sustained analytical voice that is interpretively significant as the narrator positions Eliza within a racialized aesthetic framework. The draft fuses it into 'dazzling beauty,' losing both the rhetorical rhythm and the sociological framing.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain the two-sentence ethnographic digression in close to its original phrasing before the Eliza-specific application.

findings.source_passage: this same gentleman, having heard of the fame of George's invention, took a ride over to the factory, to see what this intelligent chattel had been about. He was received with great enthusiasm by the employer, who congratulated him on possessing so valuable a slave.
findings.source_locator: Paragraph after George's introduction as factory worker, before the factory tour scene
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'so valuable a slave' delivered with deadpan narratorial irony — congratulating an owner on his chattel — is a signature moment of Stowe's satirical narrator voice. The draft absorbs it into a neutral summary, dropping the irony entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence 'He was received with great enthusiasm by the employer, who congratulated him on possessing so valuable a slave' to keep the satirical irony intact.

findings.source_passage: And so fell George's last hope;—nothing before him but a life of toil and drudgery, rendered more bitter by every little smarting vexation
findings.why_it_matters: The source reads 'rendered more bitter by every little smarting vexation and indignity'; the draft drops 'rendered more bitter by every little' and substitutes 'sharpened by every smarting,' weakening the accumulative bitterness the original phrasing conveys.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'rendered more bitter by every little smarting vexation and indignity' verbatim.

summary: The draft is largely faithful and preserves the most critical verbatim passages (the transfixed George scene, the closing jurist epigram, the wedding scene, and the 'man could not become a thing' line), but it flattens the narrator's distinctive sociological voice in the opening ethnographic digression and loses the deadpan irony of 'so valuable a slave'; three medium findings, no high-severity losses.
